# Game profiles

Each game the port knows has a folder `dm/games/<id>/`, named after the base game's title ID: Mario's is `010015100B514000`, Engage's `0100A6301214E000`. The folder holds:

- **`game.tsv`**: the game's constants, one `key<TAB>value` row each, with comments on their own lines.
- **The shader tables** that `shader_split.py` writes: `shader_map.tsv` (+ `.conflicts.tsv`), `shader_facts.tsv`, `shader_pairs.tsv`.
- **`shader_facts_manual.tsv`** (optional): hand-written translation facts in `shader_facts.tsv`'s row format, for what the machine code cannot tell (Link's Awakening: a vertex input the integer-input guess gets wrong; Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom: integer fragment outputs, which a game without a PC version has no other source for). `shader_split.py` merges it over the generated rows; since the table is on the chain, changing it changes only that profile's chain version.
- **`c1_full.tsv`**: regenerated by `c1_guard.py` after each shader build.
- **`pso_manifest.tsv`**: the prewarm seed list.
- **`vk_capture.tsv`** (Vulkan games with `shader_vk_capture`): the keys of the SPIR-V modules the game generates at run time.
- **`bf_want.tsv`**.
- **`dmsh_chain.h`**: the chain version, written by `dmsh_chain.py --header`.

Everything game-specific belongs here. Code reads the profile; it does not hard-code a game.

| Who | Picks the profile with | Reads |
|---|---|---|
| Shader tools (`shader_split.py`, `dmsh_chain.py`, `dmsh_build.py`, `dmsh_facts.py`) | `DM_GAME=<id>` | tables, `nvn_*`, `shader_*` keys |
| Host (`make -C dm/host`, `dm/gfx/tests`) | `GAME=<id>` | `gen/<id>/game_profile.h`, generated from `game.tsv` by `game.py header` |
| `dm/ios/tools/build_ipa.sh` | `GAME=<id>` | app name, bundle ID, IPA name, modules, RomFS marker, tables |
| `scripts/build_ipa_from_nsp.py` | the NSPs' title ID | everything above. With no matching profile it writes a survey, then a provisional profile outside the repository and a best-effort IPA (`--survey-only` stops after the survey) |

None of them has a default game: without one they stop and list the profiles. To query a profile:
- `python3 dm/games/game.py list` lists the profiles.
- `python3 dm/games/game.py <id> <key>` prints one key.

## Keys

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `title_id`, `program_id` | Identity. `program_id` is what `svcGetInfo(ProgramId)` reports. The game's name is not stored: the NSP script reads it from the NSP's control data (NACP) |
| `name` | The game's name, only a label for `game.py list`, error messages and the Mac window title. The iOS app's name is the game name in the base NSP's control data and its bundle ID is `org.nxnative.<title ID in lowercase>`; the NSP script's `APP_NAME` / `BUNDLE_ID` and `build_ipa.sh`'s `DM_DISPLAY_NAME` / `DM_BUNDLE_ID` override them |
| `ipa`, `app_category` | iOS app: the default IPA file name and the App Store category |
| `build <ver> <display version> <module>=<build ID>…` | One row per known version. The NSP script rejects other builds. The host reports the display version by `main`'s build ID |
| `package` | Version packed into the IPA by default |
| `shader_versions` | Versions whose union the shader tables are (base game first). All of them are needed to build |
| `modules` | Code modules rewritten and loaded, in load order. `rtld` is replaced by the host |
| `romfs_marker` | A path that must exist in the RomFS |
| `zip_store` | Extensions the IPA stores without compressing |
| `graphics` | `nvn` (the default) or `vulkan`: the game renders with Vulkan and the host implements its `vk*` imports on Metal (`dm/gfx/vk/hle_vk.m`, Hades). Its shaders are the game's SPIR-V files, translated by `dm/gfx/tools/vk_shaders.py <RomFS> <shader dir> [--ios <dir>]` into `<dir>/vk/`; `build_ipa.sh` then ships `$MSL_IOS/vk` instead of the NVN chain libraries, and the NVN shader tables stay empty |
| `mem_reserve`, `mem_alias`, `mem_stack`, `app_pool` | Guest address-space partition and application pool (`hle_svc.c`) |
| `mem_used` | Memory `GetInfo(UsedMemorySize)` reports beside the heap (default `0x4000000`, 64 MB). `SetHeapSize` checks a request against the real size of the loaded modules, so a game that sizes its heap as total − used and has more than 64 MB of modules needs at least their size here. Hyrule Warriors: Age of Calamity: 66.6 MB of modules, so the default made `SetHeapSize(pool − 64 MB)` fail and `nnMain` return at once; it sets 72 MB |
| `present_interval` | `game` (the default): frames are paced by the present interval the game sets, as on the Switch (a frame presented with interval 2 stays on screen for two display ticks; a game that keeps asking for 2 for a second gets the 30 fps target, and on iOS the display link then runs at 30 Hz; Mario 1.2.1 switches to 2 for single frames after a slow one; Engage asks for 2 on the Switch, and a rewriter cut on its 2.0.0 `main` makes it ask for 1, see `0100A6301214E000/game.tsv`). `display`: one frame per display tick whatever the game asks, which is only right for games whose logic does not count frames (D2R's runs on its own 25 Hz clock). `DM_PRESENT_INTERVAL=game` / `display` overrides it, also from `Documents/env.txt` |
| `fps_target` | Frame rate cap of the rewriter's frame step, for builds that have one (`patch_nso.py` `FRAME_STEP`: Tears of the Kingdom 1.4.3, Breath of the Wild 1.9.0), or the engine's own frame limit the host writes into game memory (`hle_fpslock.c`: Monster Hunter Rise 16.0.2, which also needs `present_interval display`). `0` (the default): the game's own step. `30` / `60`: the host decides each frame's step in whole vsyncs and keeps the frame on screen that long (`hle_nvn.c` `fstep_tick`, `nvn_fstep.h`): 1 at a 60 cap, 2 when 60 does not hold or at a 30 cap (and while a prerendered movie plays), plus one vsync while the game is behind real time after a late frame. Presents follow that hold instead of the interval the game sets. `DM_FPS_TARGET` overrides it, also from `Documents/env.txt`; the log line `frame step: game time … of real time` checks the game's speed |
| `frame_step` | `ticks` (the default): the frame step above. `legacy`: each game's method before it, for the iPhone A/B test: Tears of the Kingdom steps by the measured frame time capped at `fps_target`, Breath of the Wild runs its own interval controller with the 60 fps cuts. `DM_FRAME_STEP=ticks` / `legacy` overrides it, also from `Documents/env.txt` |
| `core_preempt` | `on` / `off` (the default): approximate Horizon's per-core preemption. When an SVC wakes a higher-priority thread pinned to the caller's core, the caller waits (at most 5 ms) until such threads block again (`hle_thread.c`). Metroid Dread's movie player relies on it; Mario's loading gets slower with it (first frame 0.6 → 2.9 s), so it is off unless a game needs it. `DM_PREEMPT=0` / `1` overrides |
| `shared_font` | What the shared-font address points at: `bfttf` (the default) = the 8-byte BFTTF header (with the "already decoded" marker) followed by the TTF, which Mario passes to `ScalableFontEngineHelper::Decode`; `ttf` = the TTF itself, which Super Mario 3D World + Bowser's Fury (SDK 10) hands straight to `ScalableFontEngine::LoadFont` (with the header the engine fails with error 403 and the game crashes looking up a glyph) |
| `device_api` | NVN API version `major.minor` that `nvnDeviceGetInteger` reports (default `55.15`, what Mario requires). Games check it and skip creating their device on a mismatch: Super Mario 3D World + Bowser's Fury (SDK 10) requires major 53 and minor ≥ 313. `DM_NVN_API` overrides. Not part of the shader chain version (only `nvn_*` / `shader_*` keys are) |
| `op_mode` | The operation mode the game sees at start: `console` (the default, docked) or `handheld`. Super Mario Galaxy uses `handheld`: docked, its pointer is the Joy-Con gyro, which the host does not have; handheld, it is the touch screen, which the iPhone front end feeds with the touches no gamepad control takes (`DmGamepad.m`). Handheld also renders at 720p. `DM_OPMODE=0` / `1` overrides, also from `Documents/env.txt` |
| `pad_layout` | The iPhone virtual gamepad's layout on first launch: `simple` (the default) = 2D (left stick, A/B/X/Y, shoulders, − / +), `full` = 3D (adds a D-pad, a right stick and L3 / R3). The layout button at the top centre switches between them in game and the app remembers the player's choice (`DmGamepad.m`) |
| `feedback_snap` | Fragment shader keys (prefixes) whose draws sample a colour attachment of their own render pass and must read a snapshot instead (`fb_prepare` in `nvn_mtl.m`). Writing and sampling one attachment in a render pass is undefined in Metal: the Mac happens to read the old content, the iPhone sometimes reads whole 16×16 blocks as magenta. Each such draw costs a pass split and a copy, so only the shaders seen to break are listed (Super Mario 3D World + Bowser's Fury: its final composite). `DM_NVN_FB_SNAP=0` / `all` / `<keys>` overrides, also from `Documents/env.txt` |
| `alpha_from_red` | Fragment shader keys (prefixes, up to 48) that read a single-channel render target whose channel mapping is exactly (R, 0, 0, 1) as (R, 0, 0, R) (`tex_alpha_red` in `nvn_mtl.m`). It was a workaround for NintendoWare layout captures: the game rebuilds each capture with its own mapping ((1, 1, 1, R) for one tagged `A8`), and the textures kept (R, 0, 0, 1) only while the host's `nvnTextureCompare` ignored the mapping (fixed, see [04](../../docs/agents/04-graphics.md)). Breath of the Wild no longer lists it; Super Mario Odyssey still lists its 26 layout shaders. `DM_NVN_ALPHA_RED=0` / `<keys>` overrides, also from `Documents/env.txt` |
| `tex_flush_upload` | `on` / `off` (the default): a texture the game fills from the CPU in place (no packaged layout, no `WriteTexels`) and publishes with `nvnMemoryPoolFlushMappedRange` is uploaded from guest memory like a packaged one, and re-uploaded when its pages change (`ft_add` in `hle_nvn.c`). Tears of the Kingdom streams all its textures this way; without it the 3D scene is black. Off by default because a flushed range in another game could cover an image a shader writes, whose GPU content the upload would replace |
| `render_cond` | `on` / `off` (the default): `SetRenderEnableConditional` / `SetRenderEnable` are recorded and evaluated at replay, and a timestamp report's counter field is 0 as on the GPU (`OP_RENDER_COND` in `nvn_mtl.m`). Tears of the Kingdom wraps its clears in conditions that skip clearing a target nothing has drawn into since its last clear; without the key every clear runs and its 3D scene is black. Off by default: other games draw everything, as before |
| `tex_dirty_upload` | `on` / `off` (the default), needs `tex_flush_upload`: a registered texture whose pages the CPU writes after `nvnTextureInitialize` without any NVN flush is uploaded as well (its pages are write-protected at registration, checked on first use; `nvn_ft_written` in `hle_nvn.c`). Tears of the Kingdom fills its ASTC terrain material arrays this way; without it the cave is magenta |
| `gpu_timestamps` | What a timestamp report (`nvnCommandBufferReportCounter`) records: `submission` (the default) = the time the whole submission completed, the same for every report in it; `segment` = the GPU start (`TIMESTAMP_TOP`) or end (the other types) of the segment the report was encoded in (the host commits a submission in segments of 64 draws, `sub_cut` in `nvn_mtl.m`), so two reports of one submission bracket the GPU time between them, as on hardware. Breath of the Wild needs `segment`: its frame-interval controller and its dynamic resolution read the GPU time between the frame's first and last report, and with one time for both they read 0 (the game kept 60 fps in slow motion when the GPU could not keep up). `DM_NVN_GPU_TS=segment` / `submission` overrides it, also from `Documents/env.txt` |
| `vconv_range` | `on` / `off` (the default): vertex attributes the replay converts on the CPU (integer shader inputs fed float-type formats and the like, `vconv_bind` in `nvn_mtl.m`) are converted only over the vertices each draw reads (first / count, or the smallest and largest index of a direct indexed draw, kept while the index pages stay unwritten) instead of the whole bound range. Age of Calamity binds whole mesh pools: in a battle that was millions of vertices a frame. Indirect draws, per-instance streams and indices with a GPU write queued on them keep the whole range. `DM_NVN_VCONV_CHECK=1` scans the indices again at every reuse and reports differences; `DM_NVN_VCONV_RANGE=0` / `1` overrides it |
| `nvn_tex_base`, `nvn_tex_slots`, `nvn_samp_base`, `nvn_img_base`, `nvn_img_slots`, `nvn_ssbo_bases` | NVN driver constant segments, measured over all shaders |
| `nvn_septex_base`, `nvn_septex_slots` | Optional: a separate texture handle table of its own, for a game that binds both kinds of handle. On hardware `nvnCommandBufferBindTexture` and `nvnCommandBufferBindSeparateTexture(s)` fill two tables of the driver segment; without these keys the host keeps both kinds in one (Mario binds only combined handles, Engage only separate ones). Monster Hunter Rise binds both, slot 0 of each in the same frames: combined handles at `nvn_tex_base` 0x20, separate textures at 0x168. With the keys, separate binds go to slots 128 + n of the replay's table (`SEPTEX_SLOT0` in `hle_nvn.c`), `dmsh_build.py` names that table's handles 128 + n, and the replay fills both tables of c2 |
| `shader_groups`, `shader_note` | `shader_split.py` source groups and the map header note (Engage: `engine` for `data.unity3d` and `Resources/`, `assets` for the Addressables bundles) |
| `shader_main_glslc` | `on` / `off` (the default): `shader_split.py` also reads GLSLC compiler outputs (magic `0x19866891`) in `main`. 13 Sentinels keeps all its shaders there; Engage's `main` has 11 that it does not use, so the key stays off for other games |
| `shader_separable` | `on` / `off` (the default): the game builds single-stage programs and combines them per draw, so the real vertex / pixel pairs exist only at run time. `shader_split.py` then pairs every vertex shader with a cover of pixel shaders that together read every input any pixel shader reads, and `dmsh_build.py`'s `vs_pad` makes every vertex shader link with any pixel shader (13 Sentinels) |
| `shader_vk_capture` | `on` / `off` (the default), with `graphics vulkan`: the game generates its SPIR-V shaders at run time (Super Mario Galaxy: Hagi's GX shaders, 3,089 modules created from its pipeline database while it shows "Initializing system..."), so no game file holds them. They are captured on the Mac with `DM_VK_CAPTURE=<dir>` (`dm/gfx/vk/hle_vk.m`; the NSP script does it itself, booting the game in the Mac host until every key the profile's `vk_capture.tsv` lists is there), and `vk_shaders.py` translates the capture folder with the RomFS |
| `shader_glslc_capture` | `on` / `off` (the default): the game compiles some shaders at run time with its own GLSLC (Fire Emblem: Three Houses: 9 built-in KTGL shaders at boot), so no game file holds them. They are captured on the Mac with `DM_GLSLC_CAPTURE=<dir>` (`dm/host/hle_glslc.c`; the NSP script does this itself, booting the game in the Mac host until every capture file the profile's `shader_map.tsv` names is there), and `shader_split.py` reads `<version dir>/glslc_capture/*.glslc` (beside that version's `RomFS`) or `$DM_GLSLC_CAPTURE`; without the folder those shaders get no translation and the tables differ from the profile's |

The translator (`dmsh_xlate/Program.cs`) still has Mario's texture / sampler bases and the depth convention built in. It uses the bases only to look up per-slot texture / image types in `shader_facts.tsv`; `dmsh_build.py` decodes the bindings from the profile. So a profile with other bases (Engage: `0x168` / `0x568`) builds as long as its facts table has no per-slot texture / image entries; otherwise `dmsh_build.py` stops, and the translator must take the bases from the profile first.

## Adding a game

1. **Survey.** Run `scripts/build_ipa_from_nsp.py` on the game's NSP folder. Without a profile it extracts only the code modules and a RomFS list, then writes `<NSP folder>/<title ID>_survey/survey.md`. The survey covers modules and build IDs, SDK, engine and graphics API markers, RomFS containers, the rewrite-site census, and imports compared with the host hooks.
   Unless told `--survey-only`, the script then writes a **provisional profile** to `<NSP folder>/<title ID>_build/profile/<title ID>/` (outside the repository) and carries on to a best-effort IPA. `dm/games/profile_guess.py` fills its `game.tsv` from the game files, each key under the reason for it (the survey lists them too):
   - identity and name, the build row it found, the largest RomFS file as `romfs_marker`, big file types in `zip_store`, `shader_groups` by RomFS top-level folder, Mario's NVN values (Engage's texture base under Unity IL2CPP);
   - `graphics vulkan` when `main` imports Vulkan functions and not `nvnBootstrapLoader`, then `shader_vk_capture on` when the RomFS has no SPIR-V file;
   - `modules`: a subsdk is loaded only when `main` imports something from it that the host does not supply itself. Under the Vulkan layer NVIDIA's OpenGL / Vulkan drivers, the Vulkan loader and GLSLC are dropped; movie modules and a GLSLC that `main` calls stay;
   - `shader_main_glslc` and `shader_separable` when `main` holds GLSLC outputs and the RomFS has no BNSH / BAHS / UnityFS; `shader_glslc_capture` when `main` also holds GLSL sources and calls `glslcCompile` in a module the game ships;
   - the memory partition. Without a system resource in the NPDM: the 4 GB layout, its heap region the pool − 64 MB − the bss of giant modules (Metroid Dread: 0x90000000). When `main` never sets a heap: a 1 GB block (Super Mario Galaxy). With a system resource and a heap: Engage's 5 GB block with the hardware pool, which the probe corrects;
   - SDK 8 / 10 NVN games: `shared_font ttf` and `device_api 53.313`. Engine presets: Hagi (`hagi.config`) gets `op_mode handheld` and `pad_layout full`.

   `python3 dm/games/profile_guess.py --check` runs these rules on every profile in `dm/games` (with the extractions under `/Volumes/T7/nsp`) and lists the keys where the guess differs.

   After the rewrite, `mem_used` is set when the rewritten modules exceed the default 64 MB (a game without a system resource). A game with a system resource that sets a heap then gets a **heap check**: it boots in the Mac host (headless, no shader libraries) until its first heap request, or 5 s into `nnMain` without one, at most 30 s (`HEAP_CHECK_SECS`). A request the heap region cannot hold (`SetHeapSize OOM`) sets the alias / heap split (Tears of the Kingdom asks for 0x86000000, which gives its hand-made 0x98000000 alias region; Wonder's 1.44 GB gives 0xc0000000), and a pool check that fails for good sets `mem_used`. The profile gets a `# heap check:` line, and later runs keep its keys (delete the line to check again; `--no-heap-check` / `HEAP_CHECK = False` skips it). Other games skip the check, so it costs nothing for them and a few seconds plus a Mac host build for the rest.

   No short run decides `render_cond`, `tex_flush_upload`, `tex_dirty_upload`, `core_preempt`, `gpu_timestamps`, `feedback_snap`, `alpha_from_red`, `vconv_range` or `present_interval`, nor `op_mode` / `pad_layout` outside the presets: they keep their defaults for a developer. A minute's boot without input counted Wonder's clears under render conditions (65,536 or more; it needs no `render_cond`) as readily as Tears of the Kingdom's, saw Breath of the Wild flush 32 CPU-filled textures with data (it needs no `tex_flush_upload`) and Age of Calamity none (its movie frames come later), and Metroid Dread's movie crash shows in about half the runs. On the iPhone, `Documents/env.txt` can still set `DM_OPMODE`, `DM_NVN_GPU_TS` and `DM_NVN_FB_SNAP`, and the pad layout switches in game.

   The shader tables, `dmsh_chain.h` and `c1_full.tsv` are written into the same folder. A second run reuses that `game.tsv` (delete it to survey again), so it can be edited by hand. `--provisional` builds from a provisional profile even for a game that has one in `dm/games`, to test the guesses: `DM_GAMES_FIRST=1` makes every tool search `DM_GAMES_DIR` first, and the IPA gets `-provisional` in its name. Tools find profiles outside `dm/games` through `DM_GAMES_DIR` (folders separated by `:`, searched after `dm/games`); `make -C dm/host` reaches such a profile through the symlink `dm/host/gen/<id>/profile`. To keep a game, move the folder into `dm/games/` and bring it up as below.
2. **Profile.** Copy `010015100B514000/game.tsv` (or the provisional profile) to `dm/games/<title ID>/game.tsv` (the base game's title ID, as the folder name) and fill in the identity, `build` rows and `modules`. Leave the memory and NVN values as Mario's until the bring-up measures them ([docs/agents](../../docs/agents/README.md)).
3. **Shader tables.** Run `DM_GAME=<id> shader_split.py … dm/games/<id>/shader_map.tsv dm/games/<id>/shader_facts.tsv dm/games/<id>/shader_pairs.tsv`. Add an empty `shader_map.tsv.conflicts.tsv`, `bf_want.tsv` and `pso_manifest.tsv` (copy Mario's headers).
4. **Chain.**
   1. `DM_GAME=<id> dmsh_chain.py --header`
   2. `DM_GAME=<id> [IOSOUT=…] dmsh_build.py <pkg> <cache>`
   3. `c1_guard.py <cache>/b-<V> dm/games/<id>/c1_full.tsv`
5. **Host bring-up.** Run `make -C dm/host GAME=<id>`, then work through the bring-up loop in docs/agents. Code that only fits one game is gated by its build ID (`dm_main_build()`), never left to run on every game.
6. **IPA.** Use `GAME=<id> dm/ios/tools/build_ipa.sh`, or the NSP script, which now finds the profile.
